<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<span class="ltx_personname">Bernie Wang

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Time series foundation models are becoming increasingly popular for general-purpose forecasting.
However, most leading models predict marginal quantiles, leaving the dependence structure of future trajectories unspecified.
This distinction matters for trajectory-dependent quantities such as cumulative demand, peak load, and event timing, yet point and marginal scores do not reveal it.
To model this dependence, we introduce PathFM, a trajectory-based forecasting model that uses flow matching to generate complete future paths.
We further distill the model to one or two steps and share history attention cache across draws.
Together, these enable PathFM to generate multiple paths for a single series in roughly the time needed for one query to a quantile model.
The distilled sampler also makes it practical to optimize a calibration loss directly.
PathFM achieves competitive marginal accuracy on the established forecasting benchmarks fev-bench and TIME.
To complement these evaluations, we introduce Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench), which augments fev-bench tasks with energy and variogram scores and downstream metrics.
PathFM achieves a higher aggregate path score on fps-bench than all evaluated external baselines.
Experiments on chaotic systems further show that our flow model sustains long-run variability, while strong baselines rapidly collapse.
PathFM makes generative time series forecasting both competitive and practical, enabling diverse downstream applications.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">

</tbody>
</table>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are a hot topic <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ansari et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Das et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ansari et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain &amp; Sen, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohen et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
The field is growing fast:
Every year, new models are released that refresh the leaderboard.
The models are commonly evaluated through point accuracy (e.g., MASE) and marginal probabilistic scores (e.g., CRPS, scaled quantile loss) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aksu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shchur et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Consequently, most of the recent TSFMs are designed and trained to produce quantile levels, which are optimized for these benchmarks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Point accuracy and marginal probabilistic scores are widely adopted for good reason: they provide an interpretable, per-step summary of forecast quality that directly supports common operational decisions such as inventory planning, resource allocation, and risk management.
However, they do not capture all aspects of forecast quality.
Other properties, particularly <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">trajectory-dependent</span> ones, are important but overlooked by these metrics.
Among many, we illustrate two important aspects:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Learning distributions with multiple modes:</span> Quantiles are defined through the inverse of the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the target distribution.
These CDFs, however, are not always nice and smooth, for instance, when the target distribution has multiple modes or sharp peaks.
With a few or a few dozens of quantiles, the resulting approximation of the CDF can be quite rough and suffer from a regression-to-the-mean issue <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
See the Lorenz oscillator example in <a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Learning autocorrelation:</span> Many quantile regression models predict marginal quantiles at individual time steps across a forecast window.
These marginal outputs do not specify temporal dependence among future values within that window.
For instance, many forecasting problems also require learning trajectory-dependent quantities, such as cumulative demand, peak load, and threshold-crossing times <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez-Diaz et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cai et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
See the solar-output example in <a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
A marginal quantile loss does not identify these joint properties.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.22358v1/forecast_ambiguity.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/251;" width="548" height="251"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Two advantages of trajectory generation.
Left: a sampled Lorenz rollout sustains variability and a two-lobe structure, while the fine-tuned Chronos-2 trace contracts.
Both use the dynamical models in <a href="#S6" title="6 Forecasting chaotic dynamics ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.
Gray Lorenz curves show the observed continuation.
Right: solar-output paths from PathFM and independent (ind.) and comonotone (com.) completions of the Chronos-2 (C2) quantiles.
Horizontal dashed lines marks each solar path’s daily maximum; black denotes the observed future.
In (g), boxes show medians and interquartile ranges across 32 paths, whiskers show the 10–90% range, and the dashed line marks the observed maximum.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Ad hoc methods have been proposed to mitigate these weaknesses, such as completing marginal quantiles under independence or comonotone assumptions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez-Diaz et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, or learning copula structures on top of marginal forecasts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Drouin et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ashok et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
On the other hand, diffusion- or flow-matching-based generative time-series models are naturally well-suited for capturing joint trajectory distributions even without these ad hoc methods, as they can generate complete future paths while maintaining temporal and cross-variable dependencies.
Unfortunately, existing generative models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kollovieh et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> achieve neither high marginal accuracy nor efficient sampling, limiting their practical utility in real-world forecasting scenarios.
This leads us to ask:</p>
<p id="S1.p3.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S1.p3.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle" style="--ltx-border-color:#B3B3B3;">
<span id="S1.p3.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_middle" style="width:369.7pt;--ltx-bg-color:#F1F5F9;">
<span id="S1.p3.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S1.p3.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Can we construct a generative time-series model that achieves both high marginal accuracy and efficient sampling while also preserving trajectory dependence?</span></span>
</span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce PathFM to combine joint and multi-mode trajectory modeling with accurate marginal forecasting and efficient sampling.
The model learns temporal and cross-variable dependence through conditional flow matching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lipman et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, generating complete future paths conditioned on history and known future covariates.
Parallel decoding distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shaul et al., 2026</a>)</cite> and history attention caching enable faster sampling with one or two model evaluations.
To narrow the marginal accuracy gap, we add a calibration loss that directly optimizes fair CRPS on generated forecasts.
The distilled sampler makes this optimization practical by allowing calibration gradients to pass through its short rollout and refine the forecast distribution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">With these components, PathFM-300M ranks <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">second</span> on the widely used fev-bench for marginal scores (<a href="#S5" title="5 Forecasting accuracy and efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          Cutoff date for the rankings throughout this paper: Sept. 26, 2026; see <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Concurrent Work ‣ Appendix A Related Work ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a> for concurrent work.</span></span></span>
On Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench), which we curate to evaluate trajectory quality, PathFM ranks <span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">first</span> for path scores (<a href="#S5" title="5 Forecasting accuracy and efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).
In a separate evaluation on chaotic systems, our sampling approach improves point forecast accuracy upon the state-of-the-art PANDA model, captures useful temporal dependence, and preserves long-run variability more faithfully than baselines (<a href="#S6" title="6 Forecasting chaotic dynamics ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).
These results demonstrate that PathFM generates high-fidelity trajectory forecasts without sacrificing marginal accuracy, making it a strong candidate for forecasting applications.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Our contributions are as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I2" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Fast and calibrated trajectory generation.</span>
We introduce PathFM, a joint flow foundation model for fast, calibrated trajectory generation with accurate small-ensemble marginals (<a href="#S3.F2" title="In 3 Fast and Calibrated Trajectory Forecasting ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).
Distillation enables one- or two-step generation, marginal-CRPS refinement improves empirical coverage, and stratified sampling reduces finite-ensemble marginal error.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A benchmark for trajectory distributions.</span>
We introduce fps-bench, to our knowledge the first dedicated benchmark for evaluating path distributions from time series foundation models on real-world data.
It reveals how strong marginal accuracy in existing models can mask errors in temporal dependence and uncertainty over trajectory-dependent quantities.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">State-of-the-art performance.</span>
PathFM outperforms leading foundation models on downstream probabilistic forecasting tasks and stays among the top on marginal benchmarks.
It also achieves the highest forecasting accuracy across strong baselines on chaotic systems.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Problem setup and preliminaries</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Forecast object and downstream query.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times C}</annotation></semantics></math> be the observed history and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times C}</annotation></semantics></math> the future.
The available information <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{I}</annotation></semantics></math> includes <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math>, observation masks, and known future covariates.
A predictive law <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\theta}(Y\mid\mathcal{I})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\theta}(Y\mid\mathcal{I})</annotation></semantics></math> supports queries about individual coordinates or a trajectory functional <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g(Y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g(Y)</annotation></semantics></math>, such as cumulative sum or autocorrelation.
A trajectory generator represents this law through <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X=G_{\theta}(\mathcal{I},Z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X=G_{\theta}(\mathcal{I},Z)</annotation></semantics></math>, where each noise draw <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math> produces one complete future path.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez-Diaz et al. (2025)</a></cite> distinguish point, quantile, parametric-distribution, and trajectory forecast products by the decisions they support.
Coordinatewise quantiles <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{\tau}(Y_{\ell,c}\mid\mathcal{I})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{\tau}(Y_{\ell,c}\mid\mathcal{I})</annotation></semantics></math> and marginal distribution parameters leave temporal and cross-variable dependence unspecified.
Consequently, they do not determine predictive autocorrelation or distributions of sums, maxima, and path-dependent events without an additional dependence assumption.
Joint trajectory samples support direct estimation of those quantities by applying <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> to each generated path.
<a href="#S2.T1" title="In Forecast object and downstream query. ‣ 2 Problem setup and preliminaries ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> compares forecast objects, computational costs, and task compatibility; <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Related Work ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> discusses related work.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.T1" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Forecast objects, inference cost, and task compatibility of representative models.</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<table id="S2.T1.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_figure_panel ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S2.T1.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S2.T1.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;" rowspan="2"><span id="S2.T1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text">Model</span></th>
<th id="S2.T1.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;" rowspan="2"><span id="S2.T1.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_text">Forecast object</span></th>
<th id="S2.T1.2.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;" rowspan="2"><span id="S2.T1.2.1.3.1" class="ltx_text">NFE</span></th>
<td id="S2.T1.2.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;" colspan="4">Task compatibility</td></tr>
<tr id="S2.T1.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.T1.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;">
<span id="S2.T1.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S2.T1.2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">Pretrained</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.2.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;">
<span id="S2.T1.2.2.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S2.T1.2.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">Marginal</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.2.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;">
<span id="S2.T1.2.2.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S2.T1.2.2.3.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">Path</span>
</span></td>

<p id="S2.T1.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_middle" style="width:397.5pt;"><em id="S2.T1.3.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Path</em> and <em id="S2.T1.3.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Cross-variable</em> refer to native joint forecast laws.
NFE counts evaluations per output block (per sampled path when applicable).
<sup id="S2.T1.3.3" class="ltx_sup">†</sup>TSFlow’s multivariate extension adds attention across features.
<sup id="S2.T1.3.4" class="ltx_sup">‡</sup>Temporal coupling here refers to the block generated by the conditional flow.</p></div></div>

</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Existing benchmarks and their scope.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GIFT-Eval reports point-forecast metrics and approximates univariate CRPS with weighted quantile loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aksu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>; fev-bench uses scaled quantile loss across heterogeneous forecasting tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shchur et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
TIME evaluates zero-shot forecasting on freshly curated datasets, reporting MASE and quantile-based CRPS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiao et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
These summaries assess central predictions and marginal uncertainty, including on multivariate tasks, but cannot distinguish joint laws with identical coordinatewise marginals.
We introduce fps-bench to address this gap by evaluating temporal dependence and trajectory-dependent quantities (<a href="#S4" title="4 Evaluating Trajectory Forecasts ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).
<a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 Finite-ensemble approximation ‣ Appendix C Sampling and computational efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a> analyzes finite-ensemble approximation, and <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Score construction ‣ Appendix D Evaluation metrics ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sections</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a> and <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Chaotic systems ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> define the evaluation metrics for general-corpus and chaotic-system prediction, respectively.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Fast and Calibrated Trajectory Forecasting</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">PathFM learns a flow over complete future trajectories, then distills it for fast sampling and refines its marginal scores.
<a href="#S3.F2" title="In 3 Fast and Calibrated Trajectory Forecasting ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> summarizes the training and sampling stages.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.22358v1/training_pipeline.svg" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/341;" width="548" height="341"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Training, post-training, and sampling with PathFM.
Flow matching learns a joint velocity field; distillation matches frozen-teacher velocities at student-proposed states.
Calibration maps eight iid draws through one fused step of trainable <math id="S3.F2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> to samples scored by fair CRPS, together with PDD supervision.
Sampling uses stratified initial noise to improve coverage of the noise distribution with a small ensemble.
Below: Flow enters after the flow-independent prefix, and history attention values are computed once and reused by separate packed future states.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Pretraining by flow matching</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Conditional flow matching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lipman et al., 2022</a>)</cite> learns a velocity field that transports source noise toward the conditional law <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\theta}(Y\mid\mathcal{I})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\theta}(Y\mid\mathcal{I})</annotation></semantics></math> over complete <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L\times C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L\times C</annotation></semantics></math> futures.
Here <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{I}</annotation></semantics></math> contains the observed history, masks, and known future covariates.
We transform targets to <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{Y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>Y</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{Y}</annotation></semantics></math> using context-derived location and scale followed by the inverse hyperbolic sine <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ansari et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
We draw <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math> independently of the future, with the same shape as <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{Y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>Y</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{Y}</annotation></semantics></math> and independent coordinates <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{\ell c}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{\ell c}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})</annotation></semantics></math>.
The mask <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> selects valid unknown coordinates, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pi_{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pi_{M}</annotation></semantics></math> restores known values and zeros invalid coordinates, and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\|\cdot\|_{M}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∥</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em">∥</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>M</mi></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\cdot\|_{M}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> averages squared error over transported coordinates.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At flow time <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>, we train <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> on the straight path from noise to data:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle X_{t}=\Pi_{M}\!\left((1-t)Z+t\bar{Y}\right),\quad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|v_{\theta}(X_{t},t;\mathcal{I})-(\bar{Y}-Z)\right\|_{M}^{2}\right]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Y</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>FM</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Y</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>−</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle X_{t}=\Pi_{M}\!\left((1-t)Z+t\bar{Y}\right),\quad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|v_{\theta}(X_{t},t;\mathcal{I})-(\bar{Y}-Z)\right\|_{M}^{2}\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">The expectation is over training pairs <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathcal{I},\bar{Y})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Y</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathcal{I},\bar{Y})</annotation></semantics></math>, source noise, and flow time.
Training uses one scalar flow time <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> per row, shared across all channels and forecast steps (<a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Backbone and input ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Inference integrates the ordinary differential equation, yielding <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{X}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>X</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{X}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, one complete trajectory:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{X}_{0}=\Pi_{M}(Z),\qquad\frac{\mathrm{d}\widehat{X}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}=M\odot v_{\theta}(\widehat{X}_{t},t;\mathcal{I}),\quad t\in[0,1]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>X</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>X</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>X</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{X}_{0}=\Pi_{M}(Z),\qquad\frac{\mathrm{d}\widehat{X}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}=M\odot v_{\theta}(\widehat{X}_{t},t;\mathcal{I}),\quad t\in[0,1].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Efficient backbone for joint generation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The velocity field uses a transformer based on T5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Raffel et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, with separate time and channel axes.
Its inputs are patches of 16 values with masks and time indices, a register token, and future patches populated by available covariates.
Each block combines temporal self-attention, attention across channels at aligned patches, and a pointwise feed-forward network.
We condition flow time via adaptive RMS normalization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and apply QK normalization and weight decay.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For reuse across paths, <em id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">late entry</em> separates conditioning from flow-dependent computation.
The first <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math> blocks use unrestricted attention over history, the register, and future placeholders, without source noise or flow time.
These representations incorporate the requested horizon and known future covariates.
Restricting history attention before this stage would exclude that future information.
Future positions then receive a gated difference between flow-state and placeholder tokens.
In subsequent blocks, <em id="S3.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">history-only self-attention</em> keeps history independent of the sampled path: history tokens attend only to history, while future tokens attend to both history and future.
Flow-time modulation acts only on register and future tokens.
<a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Backbone and input ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a> specifies the configuration.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Packing and caching.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Packed execution stores history once, with a separate register/future block per draw and masks preventing communication between paths.
Training averages four independent source/time draws per history, giving <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="4\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\times</annotation></semantics></math> flow-matching supervision at <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.5\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.5\times</annotation></semantics></math> the cost.
This sharing across paths is distinct from reusing history states across successive flow evaluations.
At inference, the first <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math> blocks run once per history and horizon; their outputs are reused across paths and flow evaluations.
The flow model can reuse deeper history keys and values across evaluations.
<a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Accuracy, model size, and inference cost ‣ 5 Forecasting accuracy and efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a> compares accuracy and inference cost.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Post-training: distillation with calibration</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Sampling a vanilla flow requires tens of sequential velocity evaluations, each depending on the state produced by the preceding step.
Distillation learns a shorter rollout, i.e., one or two evaluations.
This makes both ensemble generation and differentiation through generated forecasts practical.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Distillation.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Parallel decoding distillation (PDD) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shaul et al., 2026</a>)</cite> groups consecutive flow-time intervals into blocks, predicting all interval velocities in a block from one backbone evaluation.
We initialize the student from a flow teacher that remains frozen throughout post-training.
We divide <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> into <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J=20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J=20</annotation></semantics></math> intervals with knots <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{j}=j/J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>J</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{j}=j/J</annotation></semantics></math> and widths <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{j}=\tau_{j+1}-\tau_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{j}=\tau_{j+1}-\tau_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Each interval has an affine output head <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\theta,j}=W_{j}\phi_{\theta}+b_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\theta,j}=W_{j}\phi_{\theta}+b_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>.
All heads share features <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> computed at the block’s starting state and time, including nonlinear outputs and residual inputs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For a block of <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> intervals starting at <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>, the mean velocity advances <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X^{+}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\bar{h}_{\theta,s,b}=\sum_{j=s}^{s+b-1}\frac{\Delta_{j}}{\tau_{s+b}-\tau_{s}}\,h_{\theta,j},\quad X^{+}=\Pi_{M}\!\left(X+(\tau_{s+b}-\tau_{s})\bar{h}_{\theta,s,b}(X)\right)." <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Because the heads are affine in shared features, their interval-weighted parameter sums give a single readout per block.
One block of 20 intervals requires one evaluation; two blocks of 10 requires two.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For a selected interval <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, summing preceding predicted displacements gives <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{X}_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>X</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{X}_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, where the teacher supplies head <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>’s target:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\widetilde{X}_{k}=\Pi_{M}\!\left(X_{\tau_{s}}+\sum_{j=s}^{k-1}\Delta_{j}\operatorname{sg}(h_{\theta,j})\right),\quad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PDD}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|h_{\theta,k}-\operatorname{sg}(v_{\psi}(\widetilde{X}_{k},\tau_{k};\mathcal{I}))\right\|_{M}^{2}\right]." rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>PDD</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>sg</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\widetilde{X}_{k}=\Pi_{M}\!\left(X_{\tau_{s}}+\sum_{j=s}^{k-1}\Delta_{j}\operatorname{sg}(h_{\theta,j})\right),\quad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PDD}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|h_{\theta,k}-\operatorname{sg}(v_{\psi}(\widetilde{X}_{k},\tau_{k};\mathcal{I}))\right\|_{M}^{2}\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Here <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the frozen teacher and <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{sg}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>sg</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{sg}</annotation></semantics></math> stops gradients.
Gradients update the student through the selected head, with the proposed state and teacher target detached.
Targets are Euler velocities at student-proposed states, supplied without a complete teacher rollout.
Four packed draws each supervise one interval, with the flow-training coordinate normalization (<a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Backbone and input ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Calibration.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We refine the student’s marginals by backpropagating the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) through one fused sampling step.
Using few paths keeps this step affordable, but empirical CRPS has a bias that can favor underdispersion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Roberts, 2026</a>)</cite>.
Fair CRPS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ferro, 2014</a>)</cite> is unbiased for the marginal population score under iid sampling and finite first moments.
Let <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{\theta}(Z;\mathcal{I})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{\theta}(Z;\mathcal{I})</annotation></semantics></math> denote the normalized endpoint of a fused block spanning <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>.
For <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> iid source draws <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z^{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>Z</mi><mi>j</mi></msup><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z^{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I)</annotation></semantics></math>, set <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X^{j}=G_{\theta}(Z^{j};\mathcal{I})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>X</mi><mi>j</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>Z</mi><mi>j</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X^{j}=G_{\theta}(Z^{j};\mathcal{I})</annotation></semantics></math>.
At coordinate <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\ell,c)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\ell,c)</annotation></semantics></math>, the fair estimator is</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{C}_{\ell c}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left|X^{j}_{\ell c}-\bar{Y}_{\ell c}\right|-\frac{1}{2m(m-1)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j=1\\
i\neq j\end{subarray}}^{m}\left|X^{i}_{\ell c}-X^{j}_{\ell c}\right|." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>Y</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mtable rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><mi>m</mi></munderover><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{C}_{\ell c}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left|X^{j}_{\ell c}-\bar{Y}_{\ell c}\right|-\frac{1}{2m(m-1)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j=1\\
i\neq j\end{subarray}}^{m}\left|X^{i}_{\ell c}-X^{j}_{\ell c}\right|.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Retaining PDD provides teacher supervision while the generated endpoints are optimized against observations.
With <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{C}_{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>M</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{C}_{M}</annotation></semantics></math> the mean of <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{C}_{\ell c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{C}_{\ell c}</annotation></semantics></math> over transported coordinates, the objective becomes <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cal}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PDD}}+\mathbb{E}[\widehat{C}_{M}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>cal</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>PDD</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>M</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cal}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PDD}}+\mathbb{E}[\widehat{C}_{M}]</annotation></semantics></math>.
We evaluate trajectory quality using fps-bench (<a href="#S4" title="4 Evaluating Trajectory Forecasts ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) and report direct calibration diagnostics in <a href="#A3.SS2" title="C.2 Marginal coverage and ensemble size ‣ Appendix C Sampling and computational efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Inference: ensemble sampling</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At inference, PathFM generates <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> complete future trajectories, from which we estimate quantiles and trajectory-dependent quantities.
We stratify the initial Gaussian noise to improve coverage at a fixed ensemble size, then propagate each draw through the distilled sampler.
<a href="#A3.SS1.SSS2" title="C.1.2 Ensemble construction and stratification ‣ C.1 Finite-ensemble approximation ‣ Appendix C Sampling and computational efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1.2</span></a> constructs the ensembles.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Evaluating Trajectory Forecasts</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Trajectory forecasts should capture temporal dependence and accurately quantify uncertainty.
Marginal accuracy alone cannot establish this.
We introduce Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench) to evaluate these properties alongside marginal scores.
The benchmark combines established scoring rules into a common protocol for constructing and comparing finite trajectory ensembles.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Six complementary path scores.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Different downstream queries depend on different aspects of a path, motivating the complementary diagnostics in <a href="#A4.T7" title="In D.1.2 Temporal path scores ‣ D.1 Score construction ‣ Appendix D Evaluation metrics ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.
Following the aggregation-and-transformation framework of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pic et al. (2025)</a></cite>, we score both complete paths and transformations that expose these aspects.
Energy score assesses the distribution of level paths, while differenced energy score emphasizes local changes by scoring the initial level and subsequent increments.
Variogram score compares pairwise temporal contrasts to probe how values vary together across time <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Scheuerer &amp; Hamill, 2015</a>)</cite>.
We then apply scalar CRPS to the horizon total, maximum, and first-passage time to assess accumulated uncertainty, extremes, and event timing.
Specifically, first-passage time records the first crossing of a history-derived threshold.
fps-bench evaluates 94 fev-bench tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shchur et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, excluding those with NaN values that prevent computing some path scores.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Quantile-model completions.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Applying these scores requires complete paths, which marginal quantile forecasts do not specify.
We retain native samples when available.
To include quantile models, we construct paths from their marginal quantiles under two explicit dependence assumptions.
Sorted quantiles define a piecewise-linear inverse CDF with constant extension beyond the outer quantiles.
An independent completion draws a separate quantile rank at each forecast time and channel, whereas a comonotone completion shares one rank across an item’s times and channels.
Both laws preserve the same underlying interpolated marginals, allowing us to examine how the dependence assumption affects trajectory scores.
These two choices serve as baselines, as different dependence assumptions may yield different scores for the same marginal forecasts.
<a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Score construction ‣ Appendix D Evaluation metrics ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a> specifies the score definitions, estimators, and aggregation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Forecasting accuracy and efficiency</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate forecasts through their marginal accuracy, the path quality scores, and the cost of generating an ensemble.
The experiments establish where trajectory forecasts help, then examine how distillation and score refinement make those forecasts practical.
<a href="#S6" title="6 Forecasting chaotic dynamics ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> complements these experiments with a study of chaotic systems, with a particular focus on long-run dynamics.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Experimental setup</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Unless stated otherwise, PathFM refers to the 126M model; we use PathFM-126M and PathFM-300M when comparing sizes.
We evaluate marginal accuracy on fev-bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shchur et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and TIME <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiao et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
Baselines include TimesFM-3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain &amp; Sen, 2026</a>)</cite>, Chronos-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ansari et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, Toto-1.0/2.0 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohen et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Khwaja et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, and TiRex/TiRex-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Auer et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Podest et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
Quantile models use explicit independent or comonotone completions, whereas Toto-1.0 and Sundial <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> retain their native sampled paths.
GIFT-Eval results appear in <a href="#A2.SS5.SSS1" title="B.5.1 Model size and forecast accuracy ‣ B.5 Scaling and additional benchmarks ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.5.1</span></a>, and the full component comparisons in <a href="#A5.SS1" title="E.1 Temporal forecast accuracy ‣ Appendix E Forecast accuracy and dependence ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">PathFM and all fps-bench forecasts use 32 paths per forecast.
For PathFM, we use stratified Gaussian sources and one model evaluation per output block.
For each quantile model, we evaluate independent and comonotone completions and report the higher aggregate skill.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Results</h3>

<figure id="S5.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.22358v1/benchmark_overview.svg" id="S5.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/231;" width="548" height="231"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Marginal accuracy and trajectory quality for PathFM-126M and PathFM-300M.
Native samplers PathFM and Sundial are teal and black.
FPS selects each quantile model’s better independent or comonotone completion.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">PathFM-300M and PathFM-126M achieve the two highest FPS scores among the compared models while remaining competitive on marginal accuracy (<a href="#S5.F3" title="In 5.2 Results ‣ 5 Forecasting accuracy and efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).
The 300M model ranks second on fev-bench and third on TIME; both sizes have lower TIME CRPS than Chronos-2.
On fps-bench, both outperform TimesFM-3 and Chronos-2 even when each quantile baseline uses its better independent or comonotone completion.
Both also improve on Sundial’s native sampled forecasts across all three benchmarks.
TimesFM-3 leads both marginal benchmarks, but its lower FPS ranking illustrates why marginal accuracy alone is insufficient to assess forecast paths.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Path-dependent scores.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A5.F13" title="In E.1 Temporal forecast accuracy ‣ Appendix E Forecast accuracy and dependence ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> compares the six FPS components for PathFM and the three strongest external baselines.
The clearest gains over TimesFM-3 (the strongest baseline) occur in scores for temporal changes, horizon totals, and maxima.
These gains highlight the value of complete paths for downstream tasks that depend on temporal structure beyond marginal forecasts.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablation studies.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We study the cumulative effects of architecture and learning choices in <a href="#A2.SS4" title="B.4 Architecture and training ablations ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.4</span></a>.
The teacher–student evaluation-budget comparison (<a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Distillation and evaluation budget ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>) and inference speedup breakdown (<a href="#A3.F12" title="In C.3.1 Inference speedup breakdown ‣ C.3 Inference latency ‣ Appendix C Sampling and computational efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>) examine how distillation and shared history computation reduce sampling cost.
<a href="#A2.SS5" title="B.5 Scaling and additional benchmarks ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.5</span></a> provides additional results on GIFT-Eval.
We also evaluate cross-variable dependence (<a href="#A5.SS2" title="E.2 Cross-variable variogram scores ‣ Appendix E Forecast accuracy and dependence ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>) and test fitted temporal copulas for quantile baselines (<a href="#A5.SS3" title="E.3 Fitted Gaussian temporal copulas ‣ Appendix E Forecast accuracy and dependence ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Accuracy, model size, and inference cost</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">PathFM combines the highest FPS skill among the compared models with a compact 126M-parameter network (<a href="#S5.F4" title="In 5.3 Accuracy, model size, and inference cost ‣ 5 Forecasting accuracy and efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).
With one evaluation per output block, it generates 32 paths in 51.6 ms on an NVIDIA L4, placing it on the observed accuracy–latency frontier for path forecasts.
We compare the number of function evaluations in <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Distillation and evaluation budget ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a> and sampling controls in <a href="#A3.SS3" title="C.3 Inference latency ‣ Appendix C Sampling and computational efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.22358v1/accuracy_latency_b1.svg" id="S5.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/189;" width="548" height="189"></object>

Area denotes parameter count.
Latency is the median time to return nine quantiles (a) or forecast paths (b) per query on an NVIDIA L4, with history and forecast lengths fixed across models.
Quantile models use their better aggregate completion from <a href="#S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2" title="Quantile-model completions. ‣ 4 Evaluating Trajectory Forecasts ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.22358v1/sampling_distillation.svg" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/125;" width="548" height="125"></object>

</figcaption>
