<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ensemble size and distillation.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S5.F5" title="In 5.3 Accuracy, model size, and inference cost ‣ 5 Forecasting accuracy and efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> examines two ways to reduce the sampling budget in separate controlled studies.
On all 100 fev-bench tasks, stratification improves marginal accuracy most at small ensemble sizes: 32-path stratified sampling achieves almost the same FEV skill as 256 iid paths.
With one evaluation, the student approaches the ten-evaluation teacher; two evaluations slightly exceed its FEV skill.
This shows the power of distillation for time series flow matching models, and the effectiveness of the parallel decoding distillation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Scaling to 300M parameters.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We investigate scalability by comparing PathFM-126M with PathFM-300M.
<a href="#S5.F6" title="In Scaling to 300M parameters. ‣ 5.3 Accuracy, model size, and inference cost ‣ 5 Forecasting accuracy and efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> tracks flow pretraining; the larger model reaches lower training and corpus-evaluation losses at the same number of updates.
The larger model improves both marginal accuracy and trajectory quality (<a href="#S5.F3" title="In 5.2 Results ‣ 5 Forecasting accuracy and efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figures</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and <a href="#A2.SS5" title="B.5 Scaling and additional benchmarks ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.5</span></a>).
These gains come at roughly twice the inference latency for generating 32 paths on an NVIDIA L4 (<a href="#A2.F10" title="In B.5.2 Accuracy and inference cost ‣ B.5 Scaling and additional benchmarks ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>).
The scaling curves suggest that larger models may continue to improve accuracy.
This shows the potential for larger flow models.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.22358v1/training_scaling_curves.svg" id="S5.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/185;" width="548" height="185"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Pretraining progress on general and chaotic time series.
(a) Training velocity MSE; (b) EMA velocity MSE on fixed corpus windows for PathFM-126M and PathFM-300M;
(c) EMA mean validation sMAPE for the 75M and 126M chaotic models at horizon 256, zoomed to 1M–2M updates.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Forecasting chaotic dynamics</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Chaotic systems pose a sharp test of forecasting: can a model preserve statistical structure after losing alignment with a particular future?
We compare fine-tuned Chronos-2, PANDA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lai et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, and PathFM on point forecasting and long continuations of 135 DYSTS systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gilpin, 2021</a>)</cite>.
We evaluate PathFM with ten-step Euler sampling per 256-step block.
<a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Chaotic systems ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> gives its training recipe, and evaluation details.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Forecast accuracy and dynamical fidelity</h3>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Using sMAPE as in PANDA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lai et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, we evaluate forecasts at horizons 64, 128, 256, and 512.
Four complementary diagnostics assess continued paths: Wasserstein-1 distance to an empirical approximation of the invariant distribution, correlation-dimension error, squared Hellinger distance between normalized power spectral densities (PSD), and segment analog score.
Together, they assess state occupancy, geometric dimension, frequency content, and similarity of short multivariate segments to reference dynamics.
Held-out truth provides a finite-trajectory reference.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.T2" class="ltx_table">

<td id="S6.T2.2.7.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;">—</td>

<td id="S6.T2.2.7.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;">—</td>

<td id="S6.T2.2.7.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;">0.047</td>
<td id="S6.T2.2.7.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;">0.014</td>
<td id="S6.T2.2.7.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;">0.055</td>
<td id="S6.T2.2.7.9" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;">1.00</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S6.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">It achieves substantially better dynamical fidelity over 4,096-step rollouts than all evaluated baselines (<a href="#S6.T2" title="In 6.1 Forecast accuracy and dynamical fidelity ‣ 6 Forecasting chaotic dynamics ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).
Relative to PANDA, it reduces the four long-term diagnostic scores by 49–69%.
These gains accompany the lowest pointwise error at every reported horizon and persist when PathFM is scaled down to approximately PANDA’s 72M parameter count (<a href="#A6.SS2" title="F.2 Model size and sampler choice ‣ Appendix F Chaotic systems ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Chronos-1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ansari et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, an autoregressive forecasting model, has been shown to mimic local chaotic dynamics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
Chronos-1 achieves lower <math id="S6.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and PSD <math id="S6.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> than the quantile model Chronos-2, with higher pointwise, correlation-dimension, and segment analog errors.
These results highlight the distinct strengths and weaknesses of traditional autoregressive and quantile forecasting models.
PathFM improves across every reported metric, combining stronger point accuracy with greater dynamical fidelity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Distillation increases point-forecast error relative to the ten-step sampler.
We hypothesize that sensitivity to perturbations amplifies small distillation errors during autoregressive forecasts.
With one or two distilled steps, PathFM still outperforms PANDA on point accuracy and all four dynamical diagnostics.
<a href="#A6.SS2" title="F.2 Model size and sampler choice ‣ Appendix F Chaotic systems ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.2</span></a> examines this trade-off across model sizes and sampling budgets.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>What sampling preserves</h3>

<figure id="S6.F7" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.22358v1/chaos_continuations.png" id="S6.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/256;" width="548" height="256" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>Lorenz and Halvorsen continuations; PathFM uses one sampled path.
Each column shows a full 4,096-step portrait above its first 512 <math id="S6.F7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>-coordinate steps.
Gray curves show the observed continuation; open and filled circles mark the first and last forecast states.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S6.F7" title="In 6.2 What sampling preserves ‣ 6 Forecasting chaotic dynamics ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> pairs long continuations with their early time traces for Lorenz and Halvorsen systems.
The sampled Lorenz path retains a two-lobe portrait and sustained <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> variability, whereas the plotted baselines collapse within 256 steps.
For Halvorsen, PathFM’s sample retains the broad three-loop form, while PANDA follows a smaller recurrent orbit.
<a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Chaotic systems ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> provides further diagnostics.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Discussion and conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">PathFM combines flow matching, distillation, shared computation, and direct score refinement to generate complete future trajectories efficiently.
Its strongest gains concern the quality of complete trajectories and the downstream predictions they support.
The dynamical study shows a unique benefit: independently continued paths preserve variability that point forecasts can lose.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Several limitations remain.
PathFM does not yet support conditioning on modalities beyond time series, such as text.
For chaotic systems, all four dynamical diagnostics remain well above the held-out-truth reference (<a href="#S6.T2" title="In 6.1 Forecast accuracy and dynamical fidelity ‣ 6 Forecasting chaotic dynamics ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).
Accurately recovering the invariant distribution remains an open challenge.
A key direction for future work is to continue scaling the backbone and training data, pushing the frontier of generative time series forecasting.</p>
</div>

<div id="S7.SSx3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SSx3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S3" title="3 Fast and Calibrated Trajectory Forecasting ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> describes the model and learning objectives, and <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> provides the architecture and training recipe.
<a href="#S4" title="4 Evaluating Trajectory Forecasts ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sections</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Evaluation metrics ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> specify the trajectory benchmark, score estimators, and aggregation rules.
<a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Chaotic systems ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> describes the chaotic-system experiments and their evaluation metrics.
We will release the code and model weights to support reproducibility.</p>

<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Marginal forecasting.</h5>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Chronos-2, TimesFM-3, and Toto 2.0 provide direct marginal quantiles while sharing information across variables <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ansari et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain &amp; Sen, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Khwaja et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
Toto 1.0 instead predicts marginal Student-<math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> mixtures and samples forecasts autoregressively across output patches <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohen et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez-Diaz et al. (2025)</a></cite> distinguish forecast products by their operational uses and show that marginals do not identify path-dependent event probabilities.
PathFM represents the joint forecast through complete multivariate paths, so the same samples support marginal summaries and distributions of trajectory-dependent quantities.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Generative trajectory forecasting.</h5>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">DeepAR samples temporally dependent futures autoregressively <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salinas et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, and TACTiS learns multivariate predictive distributions with attentional copulas <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Drouin et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
TimeGrad introduces autoregressive diffusion for multivariate forecasting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rasul et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.
Flow matching learns generative vector fields through conditional probability paths <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lipman et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2026</a>)</cite>; TSFlow incorporates Gaussian-process priors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kollovieh et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and Sundial uses flow matching for foundation-model pretraining <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
PathFM shares history computation across paths and uses distillation to support fast ensembles and direct forecast-score training.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Distillation and direct score optimization.</h5>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Flow map methods learn finite-time transport and support both teacher distillation and self-distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boffi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boffi et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
Parallel Decoding Distillation (PDD) predicts multiple integration updates per network evaluation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shaul et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
DRaFT optimizes differentiable rewards by backpropagating through diffusion sampling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Clark et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Rewarded Moment Matching Distillation (RMMD) combines reward optimization with moment-matching supervision and applies unbiased sample CRPS to GenCast <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jacq et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
Its reward gradient passes through a denoising step applied to a re-noised student sample.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">PathFM backpropagates fair CRPS through the complete source-to-forecast map of one distilled evaluation.
The same optimization updates continue matching the frozen teacher’s joint velocity field while fitting the student’s marginals to observations.
Distillation thus supplies both a short path for score gradients and continued supervision from a joint generative teacher.
<a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Post-training: distillation with calibration ‣ 3 Fast and Calibrated Trajectory Forecasting ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sections</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a> and <a href="#A2.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ B.4 Architecture and training ablations ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> give the objective and post-training comparisons.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Forecast evaluation.</h5>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Proper scoring rules underpin forecast comparison <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gneiting &amp; Raftery, 2007</a>)</cite>.
Fair scores address finite-ensemble effects <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ferro, 2014</a>)</cite>; variogram and transformation-based scores expose complementary multivariate properties <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Scheuerer &amp; Hamill, 2015</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pic et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
fps-bench combines these principles on fev-bench tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shchur et al., 2025</a>)</cite> to assess temporal dependence and trajectory-dependent quantities alongside marginal accuracy.
DYSTS supplies interpretable chaotic systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gilpin, 2021</a>)</cite>, while PANDA studies pretraining across chaotic dynamics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lai et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
Together, these evaluations test the value of complete forecast paths through downstream uncertainty, short-term tracking, and long-run dynamical fidelity.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Concurrent Work</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Time series foundation models are advancing rapidly.
t0-gamma alternates temporal and variate attention to incorporate historical and known-future covariates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meyer et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
It averages weights from five fine-tuned checkpoints into one 256M-parameter model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">The Forecasting Company, 2026</a>)</cite>.
QiYao-M fuses numerical patches with text and image embeddings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cheng et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, but treats each target channel independently.
EXAONE 1.0 specializes at financial forecasting and mixes time with causal convolutions and variates with groupwise pooling MLPs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">All three models predict marginal quantiles, leaving dependence across future times and variables unspecified.
PathFM retains its advantage in directly generating joint multivariate trajectories, combining learned temporal and cross-variable dependence with fast sampling and marginal calibration.</p>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Model and training</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section specifies the backbone and the training recipe for 126M and 300M models, then examines distillation, calibration, and the architecture controls that support the design.
It closes with model-size comparisons of forecast accuracy and inference cost, including results on FEV, FPS, TIME, and GIFT-Eval.
The flow model has 125.1M parameters, and its distilled version has 126.3M including the PDD heads.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Backbone and input</h3>

<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Backbone configuration.</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The settings below describe the general-domain forecasting model; <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Chaotic systems ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> gives the separate dynamical configuration.
The backbone uses velocity prediction, ReLU activation, rotary temporal positions, and dynamic adaptive RMS normalization.
The latter applies <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(1+\alpha)\odot\operatorname{RMSNorm}(h)+\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><mrow><mi>RMSNorm</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(1+\alpha)\odot\operatorname{RMSNorm}(h)+\beta</annotation></semantics></math>, with scale and shift obtained from a shared time projection plus block-specific offsets.
Modulation and velocity readouts start at zero; the learned state-entry gate starts at <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.1</annotation></semantics></math>.
Temporal and channel attention use query–key normalization.
The Gaussian source scale is fixed at <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=0.75" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.75</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=0.75</annotation></semantics></math>.
Both model sizes use width 768, 12 attention heads, and feed-forward width 3,072.
The 126M and 300M backbones have 12 and 30 blocks, with two and ten flow-free entry blocks, respectively.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Input representation.</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following the input representation of Chronos-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ansari et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, each channel uses context-derived location <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{c}</annotation></semantics></math> and positive scale <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{c}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="A2.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{Y}_{\ell c}=\operatorname{asinh}\!\left(\frac{Y_{\ell c}-\mu_{c}}{s_{c}}\right),\qquad Y_{\ell c}=\mu_{c}+s_{c}\sinh(\bar{Y}_{\ell c})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>Y</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:2.348em;" width="2.348em"><mi>asinh</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>sinh</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>Y</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{Y}_{\ell c}=\operatorname{asinh}\!\left(\frac{Y_{\ell c}-\mu_{c}}{s_{c}}\right),\qquad Y_{\ell c}=\mu_{c}+s_{c}\sinh(\bar{Y}_{\ell c}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The scale is the context root-mean-square deviation, floored at <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Let binary masks <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> mark valid requested coordinates and known future coordinates, respectively, and let <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> contain normalized known values, zero elsewhere.
Only <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=V\odot(1-K)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=V\odot(1-K)</annotation></semantics></math> is transported.
We write</p>
<table id="A2.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pi_{M}(X)=M\odot X+K\odot A,\qquad\|B\|_{M}^{2}:=\frac{\sum_{\ell,c}M_{\ell c}B_{\ell c}^{2}}{\max(1,\sum_{\ell,c}M_{\ell c})}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>:=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pi_{M}(X)=M\odot X+K\odot A,\qquad\|B\|_{M}^{2}:=\frac{\sum_{\ell,c}M_{\ell c}B_{\ell c}^{2}}{\max(1,\sum_{\ell,c}M_{\ell c})},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">Here <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\odot" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⊙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\odot</annotation></semantics></math> denotes elementwise multiplication; batch axes are included when present.
The supervision mask excludes missing targets, known covariates, and final-patch padding.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Flow-time sampling.</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each training row uses one scalar flow time, shared across all channels and forecast steps.
For each row and draw, we sample <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=\operatorname{sigmoid}(-0.8+0.8\epsilon)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>sigmoid</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.8</mn></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>0.8</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=\operatorname{sigmoid}(-0.8+0.8\epsilon)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)</annotation></semantics></math>.
The interpolated state and velocity target follow <a href="#S3.E1" title="In 3.1 Pretraining by flow matching ‣ 3 Fast and Calibrated Trajectory Forecasting ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Equation</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, with this same <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> applied to the entire future.
Four independent source/time draws share each history, with their losses averaged and normalized by the batch’s transported-coordinate count.
At inference, all channels advance at a common flow time.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Training recipe</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Both 126M and 300M models follow the four-stage schedule in <a href="#A2.T3" title="In B.2 Training recipe ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.
Transformer weights are initialized afresh while retaining the released Chronos-2 input embeddings, which remain trainable.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>General-corpus training schedule for both model sizes.
Warmup is linear and included in the update budget.
Flow matching and PDD use constant rates after warmup; WSD decays linearly to zero.
The final stage decays linearly to zero for 126M and uses a constant rate for 300M.
EMA starts at the end of warmup and is preserved across continuation stages.
Each complete recipe contains 2.3M optimizer updates.</figcaption>
<table id="A2.T3.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="A2.T3.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A2.T3.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt">Stage</th>
<th id="A2.T3.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt">Updates</th>
<th id="A2.T3.2.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt">Peak learning rate</th>
<th id="A2.T3.2.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt">Warmup</th>
<th id="A2.T3.2.1.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt">EMA decay</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="A2.T3.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A2.T3.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t">Flow matching</td>
<td id="A2.T3.2.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t">2,000,000</td>

<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Optimization and stage transitions.</h5>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The recipe uses AdamW with <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.99)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.99</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.99)</annotation></semantics></math> and global gradient-norm clipping at 1.
Both models use weight decay 0.01 during flow matching and WSD.
An optimizer update contains 1,024 channel rows.
Terminal decay continues the flow model with its optimizer and EMA state.
PDD initializes the student from the terminal teacher’s EMA weights, freezes that teacher, and starts a fresh optimizer.
Calibration resumes the PDD student, optimizer, and EMA.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Data and task sampling.</h5>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Training uses a 83M-row dataset of real-world and synthetic time series, including both univariate and multivariate data.
Training samples contexts up to 8,192 time steps and forecast horizons up to 480 time steps.
During training, we randomly sample context and forecast lengths within these limits.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Post-training objectives.</h5>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">PDD trains the backbone and twenty interval heads on a uniform time grid, using the block-size menu <math id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{1,2,5,10,20\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{1,2,5,10,20\}</annotation></semantics></math>, on-policy states, Euler teacher labels, and tiled residual heads.
Calibration retains path-wise PDD and adds fair CRPS with coefficient one on each loss, globally normalized over scored coordinates.
The CRPS term uses eight iid paths, one parallel evaluation, and the same Gaussian source scale as flow training and inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Main benchmark results use the final EMA checkpoint after all four stages.
The architecture, distillation, and refinement controls below retain their stated training budgets.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Distillation and evaluation budget</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A2.F8" title="In B.3 Distillation and evaluation budget ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> reports a teacher–student inference budget comparison in both model sizes.
Each pair is evaluated at 1, 2, 4, and 10 sequential network evaluations (NFE).</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.22358v1/pdd_teacher_nfe.svg" id="A2.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/296;" width="548" height="296"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>Teacher–student accuracy at different evaluation budgets.
Rows show teacher–student pairs from the 126M and 295M families; columns show FEV and six-component FPS skill, with higher values preferred.
NFE uses a logarithmic horizontal axis.
Thin vertical bars show pointwise 95% task-bootstrap intervals from 2,000 resamples.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At one evaluation, PDD avoids the teacher’s sharp loss of accuracy and has higher skill scores than the ten-evaluation teacher in both pairs.
Additional evaluations give no consistent improvement.
These results show that the student preserves the teacher’s forecasting accuracy at a much lower budget.</p>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.4 </span>Architecture and training ablations</h3>

<div id="A2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A2.T4" title="In B.4 Architecture and training ablations ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> follows the cumulative design at the controlled development budget, from flow matching (R0–R5) through distillation, fair-CRPS refinement, and stratified sampling (R6–R8).
The modulation, initialization, normalization, and regularization bundle in R2 improves both FEV and FPS.
Restricting history attention in R3 enables shared history computation but reduces FEV skill; late entry and four training draws partially recover it.
Distillation then improves both scores while reducing the number of evaluations from ten to one.
R7 adds fair CRPS to the PDD objective, and R8 changes source sampling at the same weights.
Stratification improves empirical FPS from 0.5248 to 0.5329, with a paired 95% task-bootstrap interval of <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.0042,0.0131]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0.0042</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.0131</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.0042,0.0131]</annotation></semantics></math> for the skill gain.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Cumulative architecture and post-training study.
Rows R0–R7 use iid sources.
</figcaption>

<section id="A2.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.5 </span>Scaling and additional benchmarks</h3>

<div id="A2.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare the 126M and 300M models on FEV, FPS, GIFT-Eval, and TIME, as well as their cost.
Their training curves are in <a href="#S5.F6" title="In Scaling to 300M parameters. ‣ 5.3 Accuracy, model size, and inference cost ‣ 5 Forecasting accuracy and efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS5.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.5.1 </span>Model size and forecast accuracy</h4>

<div id="A2.SS5.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS5.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The 126M and 300M families contain 126.3M and 296.3M learned parameters, respectively, including their distillation heads.
Their training recipes are given in <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 Training recipe ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F9" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.22358v1/pathfm_scaling.svg" id="A2.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/236;" width="548" height="236"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span>Scaling PathFM from the 126M to the 300M family.
Panels rank nine models on FEV SQL skill (100 tasks), TIME normalized CRPS (98 tasks), and FPS path skill (94 tasks).
Native samplers PathFM and Sundial are teal and black.
FPS selects each quantile model’s better independent or comonotone completion.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS5.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS5.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The 300M PathFM variant has higher FEV and FPS skill and lower GIFT-Eval and TIME CRPS than the 126M model (<a href="#A2.F9" title="In B.5.1 Model size and forecast accuracy ‣ B.5 Scaling and additional benchmarks ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figures</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> and <a href="#A2.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ B.5.1 Model size and forecast accuracy ‣ B.5 Scaling and additional benchmarks ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).
PathFM-300M ranks second on FEV, third on TIME, and first on FPS among the baselines.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS5.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS5.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A2.T5" title="In B.5.1 Model size and forecast accuracy ‣ B.5 Scaling and additional benchmarks ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> adds GIFT-Eval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aksu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> to the benchmark suite.
GIFT uses all 97 configurations without series or window caps and with cross-learning disabled.
Against the external baselines, our 126M model ranks fourth on GIFT-Eval CRPS and the 300M model ranks third.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="A2.SS5.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.5.2 </span>Accuracy and inference cost</h4>

<div id="A2.SS5.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS5.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A2.F10" title="In B.5.2 Accuracy and inference cost ‣ B.5 Scaling and additional benchmarks ‣ Appendix B Model and training ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> adds the 300M model to the earlier 126M timing comparison in <a href="#S5.F4" title="In 5.3 Accuracy, model size, and inference cost ‣ 5 Forecasting accuracy and efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.
Both variants lie on the observed accuracy–latency frontier for path forecasts.
<a href="#A3.SS3" title="C.3 Inference latency ‣ Appendix C Sampling and computational efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.3</span></a> specifies the matched timing protocol and its limitations.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F10" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.22358v1/pathfm_scaling_latency.svg" id="A2.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/189;" width="548" height="189"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 10: </span>Accuracy, latency, and model size with the 300M PathFM variant.
Circle area denotes parameter count.
Latency is the median time to return nine quantiles (a) or forecast paths (b) for one query on an NVIDIA L4 at context 2,048 and horizon 288.
Accuracy uses the native benchmark settings.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Sampling and computational efficiency</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Ensemble size determines the precision of forecast summaries, while the sampler and its execution determine their cost.
We first describe sampling error and ensemble construction, then report controlled latency and memory comparisons.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Finite-ensemble approximation</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A finite ensemble approximates a model’s predictive distribution through sampled paths.
Forecast summaries and scores can vary with the returned ensemble due to Monte Carlo approximation.
We first separate approximation error from model error, then describe ensemble construction; <a href="#A4.SS1.SSS1" title="D.1.1 Empirical forecast scores ‣ D.1 Score construction ‣ Appendix D Evaluation metrics ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1.1</span></a> defines the scores of the empirical forecast.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">C.1.1 </span>Forecast quantities and model error</h4>

<div id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Condition on the available forecasting information <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{I}</annotation></semantics></math> and on the fitted model.
For <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m\geq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m\geq 1</annotation></semantics></math> iid paths from <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{I})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{I})</annotation></semantics></math> and a fixed functional <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> of finite variance, write <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{\theta}=\mathbb{E}_{P_{\theta}}[g(X)\mid\mathcal{I}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{\theta}=\mathbb{E}_{P_{\theta}}[g(X)\mid\mathcal{I}]</annotation></semantics></math>.
The sample average is unbiased for <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, and independence gives</p>
<table id="A3.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{\mu}_{g}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}g(X^{(i)}),\qquad\mathbb{E}_{Z}[(\widehat{\mu}_{g}-\mu_{\theta})^{2}\mid\mathcal{I}]=\frac{\operatorname{Var}_{P_{\theta}}(g(X)\mid\mathcal{I})}{m}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>μ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>Z</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>μ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>Var</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>m</mi></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{\mu}_{g}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}g(X^{(i)}),\qquad\mathbb{E}_{Z}[(\widehat{\mu}_{g}-\mu_{\theta})^{2}\mid\mathcal{I}]=\frac{\operatorname{Var}_{P_{\theta}}(g(X)\mid\mathcal{I})}{m}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Thus ordinary iid Monte Carlo standard error scales as <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="m^{-1/2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m^{-1/2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This error remains for nondegenerate queries even when <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> is the true conditional law.
Direct quantile outputs avoid estimating their reported quantiles from finitely many paths, but retain model error.
Efficient ensemble generation therefore matters for both inference cost and the accuracy of downstream estimates.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Let the finite value <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>μ</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> be the corresponding expectation under the true conditional law.
The sample average’s squared error relative to this target decomposes as</p>
<table id="A3.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{Z}[(\widehat{\mu}_{g}-\mu_{\star})^{2}\mid\mathcal{I}]=(\mu_{\theta}-\mu_{\star})^{2}+\frac{\operatorname{Var}_{P_{\theta}}(g(X)\mid\mathcal{I})}{m}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>Z</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>μ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>Var</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>m</mi></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{Z}[(\widehat{\mu}_{g}-\mu_{\star})^{2}\mid\mathcal{I}]=(\mu_{\theta}-\mu_{\star})^{2}+\frac{\operatorname{Var}_{P_{\theta}}(g(X)\mid\mathcal{I})}{m}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">The cross term vanishes because <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{Z}[\widehat{\mu}_{g}-\mu_{\theta}\mid\mathcal{I}]=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>Z</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>μ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{Z}[\widehat{\mu}_{g}-\mu_{\theta}\mid\mathcal{I}]=0</annotation></semantics></math>.
The first term is error in the model’s conditional functional expectation; the second is Monte Carlo approximation error.
This expression concerns estimation of a conditional expectation, not prediction error against one random future outcome, which also contains outcome variability.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For an event <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> with model probability <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\theta}=P_{\theta}(A\mid\mathcal{I})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\theta}=P_{\theta}(A\mid\mathcal{I})</annotation></semantics></math>, taking <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="g(X)=\mathbf{1}\{X\in A\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟏</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g(X)=\mathbf{1}\{X\in A\}</annotation></semantics></math> gives sampling variance <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\theta}(1-p_{\theta})/m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\theta}(1-p_{\theta})/m</annotation></semantics></math>.
For <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0&lt;p_{\theta}&lt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0&lt;p_{\theta}&lt;1</annotation></semantics></math>, the relative standard error is <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sqrt{(1-p_{\theta})/(mp_{\theta})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msqrt><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{(1-p_{\theta})/(mp_{\theta})}</annotation></semantics></math>, making rare-event probability estimates demanding at small ensemble sizes.
Increasing <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> reduces this sampling term but does not remove model error.
Using conditional marginals or analytical integration, when available for a particular query, need not incur the same sampling error.
Dependent or stratified draws require a different variance analysis.
The <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="m^{-1/2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m^{-1/2}</annotation></semantics></math> rate describes the approximation error of the iid sample average at a finite sample budget.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">C.1.2 </span>Ensemble construction and stratification</h4>

<div id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At inference, we approximate the forecast distribution with an ensemble of <math id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> complete future trajectories, from which we estimate quantiles and other forecast summaries.
Ensemble size controls the number of paths, independently of the one- or two-evaluation budget per path.
With few draws, these summaries can be sensitive to sampling variability.
<a href="#A3.SS2" title="C.2 Marginal coverage and ensemble size ‣ Appendix C Sampling and computational efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a> measures the effect of sample count on marginal interval coverage across all 100 fev-bench test tasks.
For more even source coverage at fixed <math id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>, each coordinate uses the midpoints of <math id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> equiprobable Gaussian bins, independently permuted across paths:</p>
<table id="A3.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E10.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="u_{r}=\frac{r-\tfrac{1}{2}}{m},\qquad Z^{j}_{\ell c}=\sigma\Phi^{-1}(u_{\pi_{\ell c}(j)}),\quad r,j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mi>m</mi></mfrac><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>σ</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{r}=\frac{r-\tfrac{1}{2}}{m},\qquad Z^{j}_{\ell c}=\sigma\Phi^{-1}(u_{\pi_{\ell c}(j)}),\quad r,j\in\{1,\ldots,m\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Here <math id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi</annotation></semantics></math> is the standard-normal CDF and each <math id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\ell c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\ell c}</annotation></semantics></math> is an independent permutation.
This assigns every rank once per coordinate without tying a path’s ranks across times or channels.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Marginal coverage and ensemble size</h3>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Larger ensembles improve marginal interval coverage at fixed model weights (<a href="#A3.F11" title="In C.2 Marginal coverage and ensemble size ‣ Appendix C Sampling and computational efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>).
Across all 100 fev-bench tasks, increasing the ensemble from 32 to 1,024 iid samples raises 80% interval coverage by 4 percentage points.
The gains diminish as ensemble size increases.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.F11" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.22358v1/marginal_coverage_samples.svg" id="A3.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/124;" width="548" height="124"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 11: </span>Marginal 80% interval coverage versus the number of forecast samples on fev-bench.
Both model sizes use iid sampling.
Horizontal references use the native 10th and 90th percentile outputs of Chronos-2 and TimesFM-3.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.3 </span>Inference latency</h3>

<div id="A3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A3.T6" title="In C.3 Inference latency ‣ Appendix C Sampling and computational efficiency ‣ PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting ofMultivariate Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> compares complete serving calls on an NVIDIA L4 with context 2,048, horizon 288, and batches of one or sixteen histories.
We measure end-to-end time, with CUDA synchronization around each call.
We report medians over 35 measured calls in seven blocks, following warmup and with randomized execution order.
Models retain their native behavior.
The marginal interface returns nine quantiles.
The path interface returns forecast trajectories, using independent completion for quantile outputs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T6" class="ltx_table">
